subject: Cognitive Science
title: Wittgenstein's Family Resemblance
description: A micro-lesson that makes Wittgenstein's Family Resemblance usable.

hook.text: What makes something a "game"? Competition? Rules? Fun? No single trait fits every game.

buildup.text: Chess has rules but no physical skill. Tag has no board. Solitaire has no opponent.

discovery.text: Wittgenstein argued that members of a category share overlapping features, like family members.

twist.text: This shattered the assumption that words must have dictionary-style definitions to work.

climax.text: Categories hold together not by one common thread but by a web of partial similarities.

quiz.question: What is Wittgenstein's family resemblance idea?
options: Category members share overlapping but not identical features
All members share one defining trait

details.summary: Wittgenstein argued that many categories are held together not by shared features but by overlapping similarities, like family members who resemble each other in different ways. No single feature is shared by all members of the category game, yet we recognize games effortlessly.
details.whyItMatters: Family resemblance shattered the classical view's dominance and inspired prototype theory. It revealed that categories can be coherent without rigid definitions.
takeaways: Categories can lack any single feature shared by all members
Members are linked by overlapping chains of similarity
The concept of game was Wittgenstein's famous example

faq.question: What is the game example about?
faq.answer: Wittgenstein asked what all games have in common. Board games, card games, ball games, and children's pretend play share no single feature. Some involve competition, some do not. Some have rules, some are free-form. Yet we use the word game coherently through overlapping similarities.

faq.question: How did family resemblance influence cognitive science?
faq.answer: It inspired Eleanor Rosch's prototype theory, which demonstrated that category members vary in typicality. Robins are more typical birds than penguins. This gradient structure, predicted by family resemblance, became one of the most replicated findings in categorization research.
